script.opening: "Thanks for seeing me. It’s really about Brian — his memory tablets, I wanted to check the dose, and he’s been a bit more confused at night. He’s the one who needs sorting, not me, I’m fine. I just… sorry. (composes herself) Ignore me, I’m just a bit tired. So, about his medication — is the dose right, do you think?"

facts.text: If gently redirected: SHE is the one struggling — exhausted, tearful, weight loss, low mood, broken sleep (up several times nightly with Brian), no respite or break in two years, lost her friends, hobbies and identity. Classic carer strain/burnout, with depressive features.

On sensitive enquiry: thoughts that "I can’t do this anymore" — needs gentle exploration of whether this is exhaustion/hopelessness or any suicidal ideation, and screening of mood. Also worth (delicately) considering whether carer stress affects Brian’s care/safety — handled without accusation.

HIDDEN AGENDA — she booked under Brian’s name because she does not feel ENTITLED to be the patient; she believes asking for help for herself is selfish and an admission of failure ("for better or worse"), and is terrified that admitting she can’t cope means Brian will be "taken away" into a home and she’ll have failed him. The deflection is permission-seeking: she needs to be told her own health matters and that accepting help is not abandonment.

If reached: she loves him, grieves the man he was, feels resentment at the relentlessness, then crushing guilt for the resentment — a normal, exhausting cycle she thinks makes her a bad wife. Naming it as normal is therapeutic.

Officially: to sort Brian’s tablets. What is needed: to gently make HER the patient, validate carer strain, screen and treat her mood/risk, and mobilise practical support — carer’s assessment, respite, carer support services, and addressing Brian’s night-time symptoms too — reframing help as sustaining her care, not failing.

ice.ideas: Brian is the patient; her own exhaustion is just tiredness and not something she’s entitled to bring.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — believes asking for help for herself is selfish and an admission of failure; terrified that admitting she can’t cope means Brian is "taken away" and she’s failed him; guilt over resentment.
ice.expectations: To sort Brian’s tablets. What she actually needs: to be made the patient — carer strain validated, mood/risk screened and treated, and practical support (carer’s assessment, respite) mobilised, framed as sustaining her care, not failing.

cues: Books about Brian but is exhausted, tearful, lost weight — the carer is the patient; gently redirect.
"Ignore me, I’m fine / he’s the one who needs sorting" — deflection and not feeling entitled to help; the real agenda.
"I can’t do this anymore" — screen mood and risk sensitively; don’t let it pass as a turn of phrase.

checkpoints.text: Gently REDIRECTS the consultation to make HER the patient (NICE NG150: actively identify carers at every contact and tell them about their right to a carer’s assessment): recognises carer strain/burnout (exhaustion, weight loss, tearfulness, broken sleep, loss of self) behind the "it’s about Brian" framing, rather than only adjusting his medication

Screens her MOOD and RISK sensitively: explores low mood/depressive features and what "I can’t do this anymore" means — distinguishing exhaustion/hopelessness from suicidal ideation — and responds appropriately (NICE NG222: screen for depression, PHQ-9 can help; NICE NG225: no risk tools or low/medium/high labels); does not put the weight loss down to stress without an examination and baseline bloods

Mobilises PRACTICAL carer support: a statutory Carer’s Assessment (Care Act 2014, s10) and a needs assessment for Brian (s9), NICE NG97 carer support (psychoeducation, skills training, information about short breaks), respite/day-care options, carer support organisations (e.g. Carers UK, local carers’ service, Admiral Nurses for dementia), benefits (Carer’s Allowance/Attendance Allowance), and involving their daughter/wider network

Addresses Brian’s NIGHT-TIME symptoms appropriately too (the presenting hook): assesses the night-time confusion (delirium triggers, pain, infection, environment, non-drug measures before any sedation, NICE NG97), arranging Brian’s own review rather than changing his medication on a third-party report (antipsychotics raise stroke risk and mortality in dementia, BNF) — which also directly relieves her sleep burden

Validates and normalises the GUILT/RESENTMENT cycle and reframes accepting help: looking after herself is what ENABLES her to keep caring; accepting support is not abandonment or failure, and does not mean Brian is "taken away"
Creates space and permission for her to be the patient: notices the tears and exhaustion, gently gives her permission to talk about herself, and does not let her deflect entirely back to Brian
Responds with warmth to the guilt and the fear of failing/loss, normalising the carer experience and dismantling the "selfish/failure" belief

Safety-nets and follows up: a Carer’s Assessment and respite plan, mood treatment/review (and crisis routes if risk emerges), carer-support signposting, a plan for Brian’s night symptoms, and a dedicated follow-up FOR HER — not folded back into Brian’s care

worked.txt: "We’ll absolutely sort Brian’s tablets, I promise. But can I stop for a second — because you’re tearful, and you’ve told me you’re shattered, and I don’t think you’re fine. Would it be alright if, just for a few minutes, YOU were the person I’m looking after? You’re allowed to be."

"From what you’re describing — up half the night, lost weight, given up your friends and the things you loved, in tears — that’s not just ‘a bit tired’. That’s carer exhaustion, and it’s real and it’s common, and it deserves attention in its own right. You have been carrying an enormous amount, alone, for two years."

"You said ‘I can’t do this anymore’. Can I ask gently what you mean by that — is it that you’re utterly worn down, or have there been times you’ve felt you didn’t want to go on at all? … Thank you for being honest with me. That matters, and I’m going to make sure you’re looked after, not just Brian."

"Can I tell you something I see all the time? People in your position love their partner AND feel worn to the bone AND sometimes resent the relentlessness — and then feel terribly guilty for the resentment. That doesn’t make you a bad wife. It makes you a human being doing one of the hardest jobs there is, without a break. The guilt is the price of caring, not proof of failing."

"I think part of why you booked under Brian’s name is a fear that if you admit you’re struggling, he’ll be taken away and you’ll have failed him. Let me be clear: getting YOU support — a carer’s assessment, some respite, a few hours that are yours — is exactly what lets you KEEP caring for him at home. Looking after yourself isn’t abandoning him. It’s how you don’t run out of road."

"So here’s what I’d like to do. Arrange a carer’s assessment and look at respite and day-care — even half a day a week to breathe. Point you to dementia carer support — there are nurses and groups for exactly this. Check what benefits you’re entitled to. And let’s tackle Brian’s night-time confusion properly, because that’ll give you some sleep back. I want to see YOU again in two weeks — a proper appointment in your own name, where I’ll examine you and we’ll do some blood tests, because weight loss deserves checking rather than just blaming on stress. And if those darker feelings get stronger, here’s who you call, any time. You came in for his tablets; I’m not letting you leave without help for you too."

f.learning: When a carer books "about the patient" but is themselves exhausted, tearful and losing weight, the carer IS the patient — gently redirect to carer strain/burnout (often with depressive features) rather than only adjusting the relative’s medication. Screen mood and risk sensitively (NICE NG222; what does "I can’t do this anymore" mean — exhaustion or suicidal ideation? NICE NG225: respond to what she tells you, not a risk score), examine her and check baseline bloods before attributing her weight loss to stress, and mobilise practical support: a statutory Carer’s Assessment, respite/day-care, carer organisations (Carers UK, Admiral Nurses), and benefits (Carer’s/Attendance Allowance). Address the relative’s presenting problem too (Brian’s night-time confusion — assess delirium triggers and non-drug measures, which also restores her sleep). The examinable hidden agenda is that she booked under his name because she does not feel ENTITLED to be the patient: she believes asking for help is selfish and a failure, and fears that admitting she can’t cope means he will be "taken away". Normalise the guilt/resentment cycle, dismantle the "selfish/failure" belief, and reframe accepting help as what ENABLES her to keep caring — not abandonment. Give her a dedicated follow-up in her own name, with crisis routes if risk emerges.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG150 (2020) · NICE NG97 (2018) · NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 (2022) · Care Act 2014 · Mental Capacity Act 2005
knowledge.summary: A carer who books about her husband but is tearful, exhausted and losing weight is the patient today. Give her permission to be one, assess mood, risk and the weight loss, and turn support into concrete steps: a carer’s assessment, respite and a plan for Brian’s nights.

points.t: NICE NG150: actively identify carers at every contact, including GP appointments, and tell them about their right to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014. Some people do not see themselves as carers. Record the caring role with consent.

Carer strain often comes with depression. Screen mood (NICE NG222; PHQ-9 can help) and explore what “I can’t do this anymore” means: exhaustion, hopelessness or thoughts of dying. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or a low/medium/high label; respond to what she tells you.

points.h: Weight loss is not just stress
points.t: Unexplained weight loss at 66 needs an examination and baseline bloods before it is put down to carer strain. Ask about appetite, eating, alcohol and other symptoms.

Care Act 2014: carer’s assessment (s10) and a needs assessment for Brian (s9). NICE NG97: offer carers psychoeducation, skills training and information about respite and short breaks. Admiral Nurses, local carers’ services and day care make this real.

A change in night-time confusion needs Brian’s own review: look for delirium triggers (infection, pain, constipation, retention, medicines) and use non-drug measures first (NICE NG97). Do not change his medication on a third-party report without assessing him. Antipsychotics raise stroke risk and mortality in dementia (BNF).

Carer exhaustion can put the cared-for person at risk. Ask, without accusation, whether she ever worries about how she is managing him; support is the first response, with a Care Act s42 referral only if there is a risk of harm that support does not address.

dg.d: Open question; accepted Brian as her reason for booking but gently redirected when she became tearful.
Caring load, broken nights, no respite for two years, loss of friends and hobbies, daughter abroad.
Face-to-face weight and examination; baseline bloods for weight loss; PHQ-9; Brian reviewed separately for delirium triggers.
Carer strain vs depression vs physical cause of weight loss; Brian’s change as dementia progression vs delirium.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm; did not attribute weight loss to stress; asked gently about Brian’s safety.
Carer exhaustion with depressive symptoms and unexplained weight loss needing assessment.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Carer’s assessment, respite and day care, Admiral Nurse and carers’ service, mood treatment options, benefits check.
Brian’s night-time confusion reviewed in his own right, non-drug measures first; guilt and resentment normalised.
Two-week follow-up in her own name; same-day contact, NHS 111 or 999 if risk emerges; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the tears, “I’m just a bit tired” and “I can’t do this anymore”, and explored each.
Idea (Brian is the patient), concern (asking for help means failing him and him being taken away), expectation (a dose check).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — believes asking for help for herself is selfish and an admission of failure; terrified that admitting she can’t cope means Brian is "taken away" and she’s failed him; guilt over resentment — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Comerford, I’m one of the GPs. What can I help with today?

It’s about Brian — his memory tablets. I wanted to check the dose. He’s been more confused at night. He’s the one who needs sorting, not me, I’m fine. I just… sorry. (composes herself) Ignore me. I’m just a bit tired. So, is the dose right, do you think?

We’ll absolutely look at Brian, I promise. But can I pause for a moment? You’re tearful, and I don’t think you’re fine. Would it be alright if, for a few minutes, you were the person I’m looking after? You’re allowed to be.
model.why: Notices the tears and gives permission to be the patient

model.text: (pause) I don’t want to make a fuss.
It isn’t a fuss. Let’s do both: you first, then Brian’s nights. Is that okay?
Alright.
Tell me what a typical day and night look like for you at the moment.
model.why: Open question on the caring load

model.text: He’s up several times a night, so I am too. I don’t get a break. I haven’t had one in two years. I’ve stopped seeing my friends. I don’t do anything for me any more.
That’s an enormous amount to carry alone. How has your mood been — do you still enjoy anything?
Not really. I’m low most days. I cry when he’s asleep.
You look as if you’ve lost some weight. Have you, and how is your appetite?
model.why: Explores the weight loss rather than assuming a cause

model.text: My clothes are looser. I forget to eat, to be honest. There’s no time.
Is there anyone who helps — family, friends, services?
Our daughter’s abroad. She rings. That’s it.
You said earlier something like you can’t do this anymore. Can I ask what you meant — worn out, or have there been times you felt you didn’t want to be here at all?
model.why: Explores the statement and asks directly about suicidal thoughts

model.text: Worn out. Completely. I wouldn’t do anything.
Thank you for being honest. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?
No. Just so tired.
I’m glad you told me. Sometimes, when people are this exhausted, they worry about how they’re coping with the person they look after. Has that ever worried you?
model.why: Asks gently about Brian’s safety without accusation

model.text: No — I’d never hurt him. I love him. I just miss who he was. And sometimes I resent it all, and then I hate myself for resenting it.

What you’re describing — love, grief for the man he was, resentment, then guilt — is something I hear from carers all the time. It doesn’t make you a bad wife. It makes you someone doing one of the hardest jobs there is without a break. What were you worried would happen if you told me you weren’t coping?
model.why: Normalises the guilt cycle and explores the hidden fear

model.text: That you’d say he has to go into a home. That I’d have failed him.

I’m really glad you said that. Here’s how I see it: you have carer exhaustion, and I think your mood has dropped into depression too. Both are real and both are treatable. Getting you help isn’t about taking Brian away — it’s what lets you keep caring for him at home.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and reframes help as sustaining care

model.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.
Here’s what I’d suggest. First, a carer’s assessment from the council — it’s your right, and it can lead to respite, day care or sitters. Even half a day a week to yourself. Would you be willing?
If it doesn’t mean him going anywhere. Yes.

I’d also like to see you in person to weigh you and do some blood tests, because weight loss shouldn’t just be put down to stress. And we can talk about treatment for your mood — talking therapy, and a tablet if you’d like to consider one. There are dementia nurses and carers’ groups who support people exactly in your position.
model.why: Weight-loss work-up, mood treatment options and carer support

model.text: For Brian: a change in his confusion at night needs him to be seen, so I’ll arrange a review to check for things like an infection, pain or constipation, and look at his tablets and their timing then. Better nights for him mean sleep for you. And there may be money you’re both entitled to — an advice service can check.
model.why: Brian reviewed in his own right; delirium triggers; benefits

model.text: Thank you. I didn’t expect any of this.

I want to see you again in two weeks, in your own name — not as part of Brian’s appointment. If your mood gets much worse, or you start having thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day or call NHS 111; in an emergency, 999. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Dedicated follow-up, crisis routes and teach-back

model.text: A carer’s assessment. Bloods and a check for me. Brian gets seen for his nights. Back in two weeks for me. And I’m allowed to ask for help.

social.t: Sole carer for two years with broken nights, no breaks, lost friendships and a daughter abroad. Isolation and exhaustion are the main risks to both of them.

Attendance Allowance for Brian (not means-tested). Carer’s Allowance usually cannot be paid alongside the State Pension, but a claim can still create an underlying entitlement that may increase Pension Credit — Citizens Advice can check. Brian may qualify for a council tax discount for severe mental impairment.

legal.t: Sheila is entitled to a carer’s assessment (s10) and Brian to a needs assessment (s9). The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries (s42) if an adult with care needs is at risk of abuse or neglect.
If Brian lacks capacity for decisions about his care, they are made in his best interests with Sheila involved. Ask whether a health and welfare lasting power of attorney exists.
Her mood and risk are her own consultation: record them in her notes, not Brian’s. Sharing Brian’s information with his carer is justified in his best interests if he lacks capacity.

professional.t: NICE NG150: identify carers at every contact and record them with consent. Book her follow-up in her own name so her needs are not folded into Brian’s care.
GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): consider the welfare of vulnerable people. Asking how she is managing with Brian is support, not accusation; escalate only if the risk is not addressed by help.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society, Carers UK and the local carers’ centre, day care and sitting services, befriending for her.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm behind “I can’t do this anymore”
Unexplained weight loss at 66 — needs examination and bloods, not just attribution to stress
Risk to Brian if her exhaustion goes unsupported
psychosocial: Two years without a break; up several times nightly
Lost friends, hobbies and identity; daughter abroad
ice: Idea: “Brian is the patient. I’m just tired.”
Concern: asking for help is selfish and means Brian will be taken away
Expectation: a check of Brian’s tablet dose

playbook.diagnosis: Carer strain with depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, poor sleep) and unexplained weight loss requiring assessment; no current suicidal thoughts on direct questioning. Husband’s worsening night-time confusion needs his own review.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’re exhausted from two years of caring with no break, and your mood has dropped with it. That isn’t weakness — it’s what happens to anyone carrying this alone. It’s treatable, and getting help is what lets you keep going.”

management.reflectIce: “You worried that telling me would mean Brian going into a home. It means the opposite — support so you can keep caring for him.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise the guilt, give permission to be the patient, and turn support into dates: assessment, respite, a day that is hers.
sharedPlan: Carer’s assessment and needs assessment for Brian; respite, day care or sitters
Face-to-face review: weight, examination, bloods; PHQ-9; talking therapy or medication by her choice
Brian reviewed for delirium triggers and medication timing; Admiral Nurse; benefits check
safetyNet: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — same-day contact, NHS 111; emergency 999
Follow-up in her own name in two weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who answer the question they were asked. The real patient is the carer, and the marks are in noticing her, assessing her mood and risk, and making help concrete.

items.fail: Spending the consultation adjusting Brian’s medication.
items.why: Brian is not assessed and the carer is missed; “does not identify the patient’s problem”.
items.fix: Promise to cover Brian, then redirect: “For a few minutes, can you be the person I’m looking after?”

items.fail: Letting “I can’t do this anymore” pass as a figure of speech.
items.why: Failure to assess risk is a safety fail.
items.fix: Ask what she means, then ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm.

items.fail: Putting her weight loss down to stress.
items.why: Unexplained weight loss at 66 needs assessment; premature closure is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face review with weight and bloods.

items.fail: Suggesting a care home or telling her she needs to look after herself.
items.why: Confirms her fear or adds guilt; she closes down.
items.fix: Reframe help as what keeps Brian at home, and offer specific support.

items.fail: Asking about Brian’s safety as an accusation, or not at all.
items.why: An accusing tone stops disclosure; skipping it misses a vulnerable adult. The proportionate first response is support.
items.fix: Ask gently whether she worries about how she is managing him, normalise the guilt cycle, then add support and review.

items.fail: Folding her follow-up into Brian’s next appointment.
items.why: Her needs disappear again; “no clear follow-up arrangements”.
items.fix: Book her own review in two weeks, with named crisis routes.

Nights, no break for two years, lost friends, low mood, weight loss, support network.

Carer exhaustion and depression, reframed. Carer’s assessment, respite, weight-loss work-up, mood treatment, Admiral Nurse, benefits, Brian’s own review.
Follow-up in her own name in two weeks, crisis routes, teach-back.

SCA_MODELS.why: Names the diagnosis and reframes help as sustaining care

SCA_MODELS.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.
Here’s what I’d suggest. First, a carer’s assessment from the council — it’s your right, and it can lead to respite, day care or sitters. Even half a day a week to yourself. Would you be willing?
If it doesn’t mean him going anywhere. Yes.

I’d also like to see you in person to weigh you and do some blood tests, because weight loss shouldn’t just be put down to stress. And we can talk about treatment for your mood — talking therapy, and a tablet if you’d like to consider one. There are dementia nurses and carers’ groups who support people exactly in your position.
SCA_MODELS.why: Weight-loss work-up, mood treatment options and carer support

SCA_MODELS.text: For Brian: a change in his confusion at night needs him to be seen, so I’ll arrange a review to check for things like an infection, pain or constipation, and look at his tablets and their timing then. Better nights for him mean sleep for you. And there may be money you’re both entitled to — an advice service can check.
SCA_MODELS.why: Brian reviewed in his own right; delirium triggers; benefits

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I didn’t expect any of this.

I want to see you again in two weeks, in your own name — not as part of Brian’s appointment. If your mood gets much worse, or you start having thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day or call NHS 111; in an emergency, 999. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Dedicated follow-up, crisis routes and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: A carer’s assessment. Bloods and a check for me. Brian gets seen for his nights. Back in two weeks for me. And I’m allowed to ask for help.

SCA_STEM.name: Sheila Comerford
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
Sole carer for her husband Brian (72, advancing dementia)
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations for herself. Brian’s record: advancing dementia, on memory medication. Their daughter lives abroad.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG150 (2020) · NICE NG97 (2018) · NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 (2022) · Care Act 2014 · Mental Capacity Act 2005
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A carer who books about her husband but is tearful, exhausted and losing weight is the patient today. Give her permission to be one, assess mood, risk and the weight loss, and turn support into concrete steps: a carer’s assessment, respite and a plan for Brian’s nights.

points.t: NICE NG150: actively identify carers at every contact, including GP appointments, and tell them about their right to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014. Some people do not see themselves as carers. Record the caring role with consent.

Carer strain often comes with depression. Screen mood (NICE NG222; PHQ-9 can help) and explore what “I can’t do this anymore” means: exhaustion, hopelessness or thoughts of dying. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or a low/medium/high label; respond to what she tells you.

points.h: Weight loss is not just stress
points.t: Unexplained weight loss at 66 needs an examination and baseline bloods before it is put down to carer strain. Ask about appetite, eating, alcohol and other symptoms.

Care Act 2014: carer’s assessment (s10) and a needs assessment for Brian (s9). NICE NG97: offer carers psychoeducation, skills training and information about respite and short breaks. Admiral Nurses, local carers’ services and day care make this real.

A change in night-time confusion needs Brian’s own review: look for delirium triggers (infection, pain, constipation, retention, medicines) and use non-drug measures first (NICE NG97). Do not change his medication on a third-party report without assessing him. Antipsychotics raise stroke risk and mortality in dementia (BNF).

Carer exhaustion can put the cared-for person at risk. Ask, without accusation, whether she ever worries about how she is managing him; support is the first response, with a Care Act s42 referral only if there is a risk of harm that support does not address.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; accepted Brian as her reason for booking but gently redirected when she became tearful.
Caring load, broken nights, no respite for two years, loss of friends and hobbies, daughter abroad.
Picked up the tears, “I’m just a bit tired” and “I can’t do this anymore”, and explored each.
Idea (Brian is the patient), concern (asking for help means failing him and him being taken away), expectation (a dose check).
Face-to-face weight and examination; baseline bloods for weight loss; PHQ-9; Brian reviewed separately for delirium triggers.
Carer strain vs depression vs physical cause of weight loss; Brian’s change as dementia progression vs delirium.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm; did not attribute weight loss to stress; asked gently about Brian’s safety.
Carer exhaustion with depressive symptoms and unexplained weight loss needing assessment.
Carer’s assessment, respite and day care, Admiral Nurse and carers’ service, mood treatment options, benefits check.
Brian’s night-time confusion reviewed in his own right, non-drug measures first; guilt and resentment normalised.
Two-week follow-up in her own name; same-day contact, NHS 111 or 999 if risk emerges; teach-back.

social.t: Sole carer for two years with broken nights, no breaks, lost friendships and a daughter abroad. Isolation and exhaustion are the main risks to both of them.

Attendance Allowance for Brian (not means-tested). Carer’s Allowance usually cannot be paid alongside the State Pension, but a claim can still create an underlying entitlement that may increase Pension Credit — Citizens Advice can check. Brian may qualify for a council tax discount for severe mental impairment.

legal.t: Sheila is entitled to a carer’s assessment (s10) and Brian to a needs assessment (s9). The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries (s42) if an adult with care needs is at risk of abuse or neglect.
If Brian lacks capacity for decisions about his care, they are made in his best interests with Sheila involved. Ask whether a health and welfare lasting power of attorney exists.
Her mood and risk are her own consultation: record them in her notes, not Brian’s. Sharing Brian’s information with his carer is justified in his best interests if he lacks capacity.

professional.t: NICE NG150: identify carers at every contact and record them with consent. Book her follow-up in her own name so her needs are not folded into Brian’s care.
GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): consider the welfare of vulnerable people. Asking how she is managing with Brian is support, not accusation; escalate only if the risk is not addressed by help.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society, Carers UK and the local carers’ centre, day care and sitting services, befriending for her.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm behind “I can’t do this anymore”
Unexplained weight loss at 66 — needs examination and bloods, not just attribution to stress
Risk to Brian if her exhaustion goes unsupported
psychosocial: Two years without a break; up several times nightly
Lost friends, hobbies and identity; daughter abroad
ice: Idea: “Brian is the patient. I’m just tired.”
Concern: asking for help is selfish and means Brian will be taken away
Expectation: a check of Brian’s tablet dose

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Carer strain with depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, poor sleep) and unexplained weight loss requiring assessment; no current suicidal thoughts on direct questioning. Husband’s worsening night-time confusion needs his own review.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “You’re exhausted from two years of caring with no break, and your mood has dropped with it. That isn’t weakness — it’s what happens to anyone carrying this alone. It’s treatable, and getting help is what lets you keep going.”

management.reflectIce: “You worried that telling me would mean Brian going into a home. It means the opposite — support so you can keep caring for him.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise the guilt, give permission to be the patient, and turn support into dates: assessment, respite, a day that is hers.
sharedPlan: Carer’s assessment and needs assessment for Brian; respite, day care or sitters
Face-to-face review: weight, examination, bloods; PHQ-9; talking therapy or medication by her choice
Brian reviewed for delirium triggers and medication timing; Admiral Nurse; benefits check
safetyNet: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — same-day contact, NHS 111; emergency 999
Follow-up in her own name in two weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by candidates who answer the question they were asked. The real patient is the carer, and the marks are in noticing her, assessing her mood and risk, and making help concrete.

items.fail: Spending the consultation adjusting Brian’s medication.
items.why: Brian is not assessed and the carer is missed; “does not identify the patient’s problem”.
items.fix: Promise to cover Brian, then redirect: “For a few minutes, can you be the person I’m looking after?”

items.fail: Letting “I can’t do this anymore” pass as a figure of speech.
items.why: Failure to assess risk is a safety fail.
items.fix: Ask what she means, then ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm.

items.fail: Putting her weight loss down to stress.
items.why: Unexplained weight loss at 66 needs assessment; premature closure is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face review with weight and bloods.

items.fail: Suggesting a care home or telling her she needs to look after herself.
items.why: Confirms her fear or adds guilt; she closes down.
items.fix: Reframe help as what keeps Brian at home, and offer specific support.

items.fail: Asking about Brian’s safety as an accusation, or not at all.
items.why: An accusing tone stops disclosure; skipping it misses a vulnerable adult. The proportionate first response is support.
items.fix: Ask gently whether she worries about how she is managing him, normalise the guilt cycle, then add support and review.

items.fail: Folding her follow-up into Brian’s next appointment.
items.why: Her needs disappear again; “no clear follow-up arrangements”.
items.fix: Book her own review in two weeks, with named crisis routes.
